pablo-picasso: Pablo Ruiz Picasso was born on 25 October 1881 in Málaga, Andalusia, the first child of José Ruiz y Blasco and María Picasso y López. His father was a painter of birds and other game and a professor at the School of Crafts. According to his mother, his first word was "piz, piz", short for lápiz, the Spanish word for pencil. From the age of seven he was trained by his father, a traditional academic artist, in figure drawing and oil painting. The family moved to A Coruña in 1891, and an apocryphal story relates that his father, seeing the precision of the thirteen-year-old's technique, felt his son had surpassed him.

His career as a painter can be said to have begun by 1894. The academic realism of the mid-1890s appears in The First Communion (1896), and a Modernist period followed in 1899–1900. After 1906 the Fauvist work of Henri Matisse pushed him towards more radical styles, beginning a rivalry between the two. The commonly accepted periods are the Blue Period (1901–1904), the Rose Period (1904–1906), the African-influenced Period (1907–1909), Analytic Cubism (1909–1912) and Synthetic Cubism (1912–1919). His works include Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) and Guernica (1937). From 1909 to 1928 he made sculptural constructions from diverse materials, such as Guitar (1912) in sheet metal and wire. In 1944 he joined the French Communist Party, and he remained a member until his death.

Picasso died on 8 April 1973 in Mougins, France, of a heart attack, having painted until 3 a.m. the night before. He died without a will, which led to a feud over his estate. At his death there were more than 45,000 unsold works in his estate, among them 1,885 paintings, 1,228 sculptures and 3,222 ceramics. In 1971 he was the first living artist honoured with an exhibition in the Grand Gallery of the Louvre, for his 90th birthday.
pacific-ocean: The Pacific is the largest and deepest of Earth's five oceanic divisions. It covers about 165,250,000 square kilometres, taking the definition with an Antarctic southern border, which is about 46% of Earth's water surface. Its mean depth is 4,000 metres, and the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at 10,928 metres, is the deepest known point in the world. More than 25,000 islands rise above its surface, many of them the remains of volcanoes, and the Ring of Fire, a belt of explosive volcanism above subduction zones, surrounds it.

Modern humans first reached the western Pacific around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. They crossed from Sundaland to Sahul, a sea journey of at least 80 kilometres, to reach Australia, probably on large bamboo rafts, although the level of maritime technology is not known with certainty. Settlement of Buka by 32,000 years ago and Manus by 25,000 years ago confirms their seafaring skill. Their descendants include the Negritos, Melanesians and Indigenous Australians.

In 1513 the Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama and sighted what he called the Mar del Sur, the Southern Sea. The present name was given by Ferdinand Magellan during the Spanish circumnavigation of 1520, when he met favourable winds and called it Mar Pacífico, the peaceful sea. From 1946 to 1958 the Marshall Islands served as the Pacific Proving Grounds designated by the United States, where 67 nuclear tests were conducted.

The Pacific is divided by the equator into the North and South Pacific. Its marginal seas include the Philippine Sea, the South China Sea, the East China Sea, the Sea of Japan, the Sea of Okhotsk, the Bering Sea, the Tasman Sea and the Coral Sea. The Bering Strait joins it to the Arctic Ocean, and the Drake Passage and Strait of Magellan link it to the Atlantic. It is the only ocean mostly bounded by subduction zones.
pakistan: Pakistan is bounded by the Arabian Sea on the south and shares land borders with India to the east, Afghanistan to the west, Iran to the southwest and China to the northeast. The Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip of Afghanistan, separates it from Tajikistan. It lies where the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates meet, a region of high seismic activity.

The country is divided into three major geographic areas: the northern highlands, the Indus River plain and the Balochistan Plateau. The highlands include the Karakoram, Hindu Kush and Pamir ranges and five of the fourteen peaks over 8,000 metres, among them K2 at 8,611 metres. The 1,609 km Indus River and its tributaries cross the country from Kashmir to the Arabian Sea and sustain the alluvial plains of Punjab and Sindh.

The earliest known stone tools in the region, about 2 million years old, were found in the Soan Valley. The Neolithic site of Mehrgarh dates from 7000 to 4300 BCE, and the Indus Valley Civilisation included Mohenjo-daro and Harappa. After its decline, semi-nomadic Indo-European Aryans migrated into the subcontinent around 2000 BCE, and the Gandhara civilisation later flourished at the crossroads of India, Central Asia and the Middle East.

The western regions became part of the Achaemenid Empire around 517 BCE, and Alexander the Great conquered the region in 326 BCE, defeating King Porus at Jhelum. The Mauryas ruled from 322 BCE to 185 BCE, and Ashoka introduced Buddhism. The Indo-Greek Kingdom founded by Demetrius of Bactria included Gandhara and Punjab, and Greco-Buddhist culture flourished under Menander. Later powers included the Kushan, the Ghaznavids, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, and the British Raj from 1858 to 1947.

Pakistan gained independence in 1947 through the partition of British India, which was accompanied by mass migration and loss of life. It adopted a republican constitution in 1956, and East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh in 1971 after a nine-month civil war. The 1973 constitution established a parliamentary system. Military rule governed in 1958 to 1971, 1977 to 1988 and 1999 to 2008, and the first successful democratic transition took place in May 2013.

The 2023 census counted 247,541,947 people, and the population grew more than sevenfold between 1951 and 2023. The country is ethnically and linguistically diverse and has a very young population, with a median age of 19. Its legislature has a 96-member Senate and a 336-member National Assembly.
palau: Palau is an archipelago of about 340 islands in the western Pacific Ocean, the western part of the Caroline Islands, with a total area of 466 square kilometres. Its most populous islands are Angaur, Babeldaob, Koror and Peleliu, and about two-thirds of the people live on Koror. North of them lies the coral atoll of Kayangel, and west lie about 200 uninhabited Rock Islands. A remote group of six Southwest Islands, some 604 kilometres away, make up the states of Hatohobei and Sonsorol.

The Palauan name for the islands, Belau, derives from the word for village, beluu, or from aibebelau, meaning indirect replies, which relates to a creation myth. The name Palau came into English from the Spanish Los Palaos through German. An older English name was the Pelew Islands.

The islands were first settled in the 3rd or 2nd millennium BCE by Austronesian peoples, most likely from what is now the Philippines or Indonesia. In December 1696 sailors from the Caroline Islands were stranded on Samar, where the missionary Paul Klein met them. They showed him with pebbles the position and size of their islands, and he drew from this the first European map of the Palau area.

The islands became part of the Spanish East Indies in 1885. After Spain's defeat in the Spanish-American War they were sold to Germany in 1899 and administered as part of German New Guinea. After the First World War they fell within the Japanese-ruled South Seas Mandate of the League of Nations. In the Second World War American and Japanese troops fought in the Mariana and Palau Islands campaign, including the major Battle of Peleliu.

In 1947 Palau became part of the United States-governed Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. A referendum in 1978 rejected joining the Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau adopted a constitution in 1981. It gained full sovereignty in 1994 under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, and the United Nations General Assembly admitted it on 15 December 1994.

The Republic of Palau is a presidential republic with a bicameral Palau National Congress. Its capital, Ngerulmud, is on Babeldaob, the largest island, and its most populous city is Koror. The official languages are Palauan and English, and the currency is the United States dollar. Palauan society follows a strict matrilineal system, seen in funerals, marriages, inheritance and the passing of traditional titles.
palk-strait: The strait stretches for about 137 km and is between 64 and 137 km wide. Its waters are shallow: around the shoals of Ram Setu they are typically only 1 to 3 metres deep, the central part is typically around 20 metres deep, and the greatest depth is 35 metres. To the north, in the Bay of Bengal, the waves are mostly swells, while in Palk Bay to the south they are mostly smaller wind waves. In the Hindu epic Ramayana the shoals are part of a bridge built by the vanara army of Rama to rescue his wife Sita from the Asura king Ravana.

During the Last Glacial Period, when sea levels fell to as much as 120 metres below their present values, the whole of the shallow strait was dry land. It was submerged again as the sea rose during the Holocene, by around 7,000 years ago.

The construction of a shipping channel through the strait was first proposed to the British government of India in 1860. Pamban Island was linked to the Indian mainland by the Pamban Bridge, opened for traffic on 24 February 1914. Trains ran from Madras to Dhanushkodi at the southern tip of the island, where a ferry crossed to Talaimannar on Mannar Island and another train carried passengers on to Colombo. The railway line to Dhanushkodi was destroyed in the 1964 Dhanushkodi cyclone together with a passenger train, killing around 200 people. A ferry between Rameswaram and Talaimannar continued into the 1970s and was discontinued by the Indian government in 1984.

The shallows, small islands and reefs make the strait difficult for large ships, though fishing boats and small craft navigate it. The Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project, commissioned by the Government of India in 2005 to dredge a channel, met opposition on religious grounds. A road bridge beside the Pamban Bridge was opened in 1988, and a new railway bridge was completed in 2024 after rail traffic on the old bridge was suspended permanently in February 2023 over concerns about its stability. A combined undersea tunnel and bridge linking India and Sri Lanka, the Palk Strait Bridge, was first discussed in 2002 and has been examined several times since.
pandara-vanniyan: Kulasegaram Vairamuthu Pandara Vanniyan was a native of the Vanni and is said to have reigned there from 1785. Much about his family is unclear, but reports give him a sister, Nallanachal Vanniyan, and two younger brothers who served as his minister and his commander. He married into the family of Kumarasinghe Maha Vanniya of Nuwara Wewa, and so gained political power in the southern Vanni as well as the north. He is said to have lived at Kumulamunai, in the present Mullaitivu District.

The Vanni served as a buffer zone between the north and south of Sri Lanka. After the Portuguese captured the Jaffna Kingdom in 1621 the region was under their nominal control, and around 1782 the Dutch defeated the Vanniar chieftains.

Pandara Vanniyan is said to have defeated the Dutch officer Lieutenant von Driberg several times. Against the British, the Vanniars carried on a predatory warfare in Mannar and Trincomalee and reached the Jaffna Peninsula, and the British built forts to keep them at bay. In alliance with the Kandy Kingdom he rose to expel the British from his district. On 25 August 1803 he attacked the Government House at Mullaitivu, drove out the garrison under Captain Edward Mudge of the 19th Regiment and seized the fort and its cannons. He then overran the northern districts as far as Elephant Pass.

He turned from conventional warfare to guerrilla tactics, but the British organised a three-pronged attack from Jaffna, Mannar and Trincomalee. Von Driberg, who had stayed on after the British ousted the Dutch, defeated him on 31 October 1803 at Katsilaimadu, capturing a cannon given to him by the Kandyan king Sri Wickrema Rajasinghe. His houses were burned and his people dispersed into the jungle and out of the Vanni.

No longer a ruler, Pandara Vanniyan withdrew to areas near the Kandy Kingdom. Accounts of his end differ: by one he died fighting the British, by another he remained there until September 1810, when British forces ambushed him, and later died of his injuries. Von Driberg set up a granite monument at Katsilaimadu recording the defeat; in 2010 it was found broken. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa declared him a national hero in 1982, and a statue stands in Vavuniya. Tamil nationalists honour him as an epic hero, and he is the subject of a novel by M. Karunanidhi and of a play by Mullaimani Ve Cuppiramaniyam that won a prize from the Ceylon Art Council in 1964.
papua-new-guinea: The country covers 462,840 km2 and includes a large mainland and hundreds of islands in Melanesia, north of Australia. It lies where the north-moving Indo-Australian plate meets the west-moving Pacific plate, which gives it a highly variable geography, active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes. Mountains cover at least 72% of the country, and the highest point is Mount Wilhelm, at 4,509 metres. The Torres Strait, 152 kilometres wide, separates it from Australia's Cape York Peninsula. This terrain helps explain why the population is largely rural and divided into many small communities.

Archaeological evidence indicates that modern humans first reached what became New Guinea around 42,000 to 45,000 years ago. Agriculture was developed independently in the New Guinea highlands around 7000 BCE, making it one of the few areas where people domesticated plants without outside influence. Austronesian-speaking peoples of the Lapita culture had reached the Bismarck Archipelago by about 3,300 years ago. Communities were linked by trade, and bananas and sugarcane probably passed from New Guinea to other regions along these networks, but each community otherwise functioned largely independently.

European names for the island date from the 16th century: Jorge de Menezes called it Ilhas dos Papuas in 1526, and Yñigo Ortiz de Retez named it Nueva Guinea in 1545. In 1884 the eastern half was divided between German New Guinea in the north and British New Guinea in the south. The British territory was ceded to Australia in 1902 and became the Territory of Papua. Australia occupied German New Guinea during the First World War and then ruled it as a League of Nations mandate. The two territories were united in 1949, after fierce fighting there in World War II, and the country became independent in 1975. Europeans brought together communities that had sometimes been hostile or had no relationship at all.

Papua New Guinea is a Commonwealth realm with a governor-general representing the monarch and a unicameral National Parliament of 118 seats, in a Westminster system. Its capital and largest city is Port Moresby. There are 840 known spoken languages, the most of any country, and English and Tok Pisin serve as common languages. Most people live in customary communities, and the constitution protects traditional communities and lifestyles.
paraguay: Paraguay lies between latitudes 19° and 28°S in the central region of South America and is divided by the Río Paraguay into two regions. The eastern region has mostly grassy plains and wooded hills, while the western region, known as the Chaco and part of the Gran Chaco, has mostly low, marshy plains. The far eastern forest belt receives an average of 170 centimetres of rain a year, the western Chaco no more than 50 centimetres. Although landlocked, Paraguay reaches the Atlantic Ocean by the Paraná–Paraguay Waterway, a system of navigable channels shared by five countries.

The Guaraní had lived in eastern Paraguay for at least a millennium when the Spanish arrived. The Gran Chaco in the west was inhabited by nomads, of whom the Guaycuru peoples were most prominent, and the Paraguay River roughly divided the agricultural Guaraní from them. The Mbayá were known for their warrior traditions and were not fully pacified until the late 19th century. Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded Asunción on 15 August 1537, and it became the centre of the Spanish colonial province of Paraguay.

In the eighteenth century Jesuit missions developed reductions to gather Guaraní populations and protect them from virtual slavery by Spanish settlers and Portuguese slave raiders, the bandeirantes. The reducciones flourished in eastern Paraguay for about 150 years, until the Spanish Crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Paraguay overthrew the local Spanish administration on 14 May 1811. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, nicknamed El Supremo, ruled from 1814 until his death in 1840 with very little outside contact, intending a utopian society based on Rousseau's Social Contract. The Triple Alliance War of 1864 to 1870 cost the country half its prewar population and around a quarter to a third of its territory. Paraguay then prevailed in the Chaco War with Bolivia of 1932 to 1935.

Asunción is the capital and largest city. Paraguay is a unitary presidential republic of seventeen departments and a capital district. The population was 6,109,944 at the 2022 census, and most people live in the east. Paraguayan culture is a fusion of European and Southern Guaraní traditions: more than 80% of Paraguayans speak both Spanish and Guaraní. The ruins of two eighteenth-century Jesuit missions, La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Paraguay is a founding member of Mercosur, the United Nations and the Organization of American States.
paris: Paris lies in northern central France, in a north-bending arc of the river Seine, whose crest includes two islands, the Île Saint-Louis and the larger Île de la Cité, which form the oldest part of the city. The Seine's mouth on the English Channel is about 375 kilometres downstream. The city is relatively flat, with its lowest point 35 metres above sea level, and the highest of its hills, Montmartre, rises to 130 metres. Excluding the outlying parks, it covers an oval of about 87 square kilometres, enclosed by the 35-kilometre ring road, the Boulevard Périphérique, and since an annexation in 1860 it has had 20 arrondissements.

The Parisii, a Gallic tribe, inhabited the Paris area from around the middle of the 3rd century BCE. A major north–south trade route crossed the Seine on the Île de la Cité, which gradually became an important trading centre, and the Parisii traded with river towns as far away as the Iberian Peninsula and minted their own coins.

Julius Caesar conquered the Paris Basin for the Roman Republic in 52 BCE, and the Roman town of Lutetia grew on the Left Bank into a prosperous city with a forum, baths, temples, theatres and an amphitheatre. By the end of the Western Roman Empire it was known as Parisius. According to legend, Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, introduced Christianity in the middle of the 3rd century CE and was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre.

For almost all of its history, except for a few brief periods, Paris was governed directly by representatives of the king, emperor or president of France. In the 17th century the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture was established in 1648, and urbanism laws have been strictly controlled since the early 17th century. Between 1853 and 1870 Napoleon III and his Prefect of the Seine, Baron Haussmann, rebuilt the city centre, creating wide boulevards, standard facades of cream-grey Paris stone and major parks around the centre.

Paris is the capital and largest city of France, with a city population of 2.04 million and a metropolitan population of 13.3 million. The National Assembly granted it municipal autonomy in 1974, and Jacques Chirac became its first elected mayor in March 1977. Its population peaked at 2.9 million in 1921. In the 19th and early 20th centuries artists including Manet, Monet and Renoir worked there, and Impressionism, Cubism and Art Deco all evolved in the city. It hosts UNESCO, whose headquarters have been there since November 1958, and the OECD, and it has hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924 and 2024.
pataliputra: Pataliputra stood where the Ganges, the Gandhaka and the Son rivers met, a position that made it a water fort, or jaldurga, and let it dominate the river trade of the Indo-Gangetic Plain. One traditional etymology derives the name from the pāṭalī tree; another makes it the son of Pāṭali, daughter of a Raja Sudarsan. The city was also called Kusumapura, city of flowers. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, who lived there under the Maurya Empire and called it Palibothra, described a city in the shape of a parallelogram, surrounded by a ditch and a wall with 570 towers and 64 gates. Strabo adds that the walls were of wood.

The place began as a village, Pataligrama, fortified by the Magadha ruler Ajatashatru; the date given is 490 BCE. Jain and Hindu sources name his son Udayabhadra as the king who moved the capital there from Rajgriha. Archaeological evidence shows urban growth no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE. Under Ashoka it was one of the world's largest cities, with an estimated population of 150,000 to 400,000, and early Buddhist texts record the Third Buddhist council there.

Faxian, visiting about 400, found the people rich and described hospitals where the poor were treated without charge. Xuanzang in 637 found the old city in ruins, with a small walled town of about 1,000 people by the river. Suggested causes of the decline are a shift in the course of the Ganges, a flood on the Son recorded in a later Jain work and placed in the late 500s, and destruction by Hunas in the early 500s. An inscription of the Pala king Dharmapala from the early 800s describes it as a river port and royal camp. Sher Shah Suri later made it his capital under the name Patna.

Much of the ancient city lies buried under modern Patna. Its site was first identified in modern times by Laurence Waddell in 1892, and excavations have been made at Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan. They have found stretches of the wooden palisade over several kilometres, but no stone fortifications. At Kumhrar the remains thin out from the 300s and stop about 600, and a thick layer of ash in the hall of 80 pillars suggests that it was burnt.
paul-doumer: Joseph Athanase Doumer, commonly known as Paul, was born on 22 March 1857 at Aurillac in the Cantal department into a family of modest means. A former student of the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, he became a professor of mathematics at Mende in 1877 and taught at Remiremont from 1879 to 1883, leaving on health grounds to become chief editor of a regional newspaper, the Courrier de l'Aisne. In 1878 he married Blanche Richel. They had eight children, four of whom were killed in the First World War. He was initiated into Freemasonry in 1879 and became Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient de France in 1892.

Doumer entered politics in 1885 as chef de cabinet to Charles Floquet, president of the Chamber of Deputies, and was elected Radical deputy for the Aisne in 1888. Defeated in 1889, he was returned in 1890 by the arrondissement of Auxerre. As minister of finance in 1895–1896 he tried without success to introduce an income tax.

When he arrived in Indochina the colonies were losing millions of francs a year, and his taxes were meant to put them on a paying basis. Vietnamese, Cambodians and Laotians who could not or would not pay lost their houses and land and often became day labourers. He made Indochina a market for French products and a field for French investment. In 1898 he persuaded the French government to approve the railway to Yunnan, with a view to annexing the south of that province.

Back in France he was elected deputy for Laon, refused to support the ministry of Émile Combes and led a group of dissident Radicals that eventually helped bring it down. He was president of the Chamber from 1902 to 1905, minister of finance again in 1925 and president of the Senate from 1927. On 13 May 1931 he was elected president of the Republic, defeating the better-known Aristide Briand.

On 6 May 1932, at the opening of a book fair at the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild in Paris, Doumer was shot by Paul Gorguloff, a Russian émigré, while talking to the author Claude Farrère. He died in hospital at 04:37 on 7 May, the second French president to be assassinated and the first to be shot. Gorguloff wrote that the act was a protest on behalf of exiled White Russians and against France's relations with the Soviet Union; he was guillotined four months later. Doumer wrote L'Indo-Chine française (1904) and Le Livre de mes fils (1906).
persian-language: Modern Persian is a continuation of Middle Persian, an official language of the Sasanian Empire (224–651 CE), which was itself a continuation of Old Persian, used in the Achaemenid Empire (550–330 BCE). It originated in the region of Fars in southwestern Iran. Old Persian is attested in cuneiform inscriptions from the 6th to the 4th century BCE, the oldest being the Behistun Inscription from the time of King Darius I (reigned 522–486 BCE). Middle Persian is attested in Pahlavi and Manichaean scripts, and New Persian literature was first recorded in the ninth century, after the Muslim conquest of Persia. Gernot Windfuhr treats New Persian as an evolution of both earlier stages, but states that none of the known Middle Persian dialects is its direct predecessor.

Persian belongs to the Western Iranian group of the Iranian languages. It has three standard varieties: Iranian Persian, Dari in Afghanistan and Tajiki in Tajikistan, all based on classic Persian literature and mutually intelligible to a relatively high degree. Iranian Persian and Dari are written in the Persian alphabet, a modified form of the Arabic alphabet; after the Arab conquest it took about 200 years before Persians adopted the Arabic script in place of Pahlavi. Tajiki is written in a Cyrillic alphabet.

Modern Persian has no grammatical gender and its usual word order is subject–object–verb. Its core vocabulary is of Middle Persian origin, but it also contains a considerable number of Arabic loanwords. John R. Perry estimates that about 20 percent of everyday vocabulary, and around 25 percent of that of classical and modern literature, is of Arabic origin.

Persian was the first language to break the monopoly of Arabic on writing in the Muslim world, and Persian poetry became a tradition in many eastern courts. It served as a language of bureaucracy even for non-native speakers, among them the Ottomans in Anatolia, the Delhi Sultanates and Mughals in the Indian subcontinent, and the Pashtuns in Afghanistan. It influenced Turkic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek and Indo-Aryan languages, as well as other Iranian ones. Works written in it include the Shahnameh by Ferdowsi, the works of Rumi, the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, the Divân of Hafez and the Gulistan and Bustan by Saadi Shirazi. Approximately 130 million people speak it worldwide.
peru: Peru covers 1,285,216 km2 on the Pacific coast of South America, the third-largest country on the continent. The Andes run parallel to the ocean and define three traditional regions: the costa, a narrow and largely arid coastal plain; the sierra, the highlands, which include the Altiplano and the highest peak, Huascarán at 6,768 metres; and the selva, the Amazon rainforest, which covers almost 60 percent of the country.

The Amazon basin covers 75% of Peruvian territory, and Lake Titicaca, shared with Bolivia, is the largest lake in South America. The name may derive from Birú, a local ruler near the Bay of San Miguel in Panama, and the Capitulation of Toledo of 1529 gave it legal status as the name of the province that was the Inca Empire.

The earliest evidence of people in Peruvian territory, about 12,500 BCE, comes from Huaca Prieta. The Caral-Supe civilization flourished on the coast between 3,000 and 1,800 BCE, and the Chavín culture, from 1500 to 300 BCE, was probably more a religious than a political phenomenon. Later coastal cultures included the Paracas, Nazca, Moche and Chimu. The Chimu flourished from about 1140 to 1450 as a loose confederation of walled cities with its capital at Chan Chan, and in the highlands the Tiahuanaco and Wari cultures developed large urban settlements between 500 and 1000 CE.

The Spanish Empire conquered the region in the 16th century, and Charles V established a viceroyalty, the Kingdom of Peru, with its capital at Lima. According to the historian Noble David Cook, the Amerindian population fell from nearly 5–9 million in the 1520s to around 600,000 in 1620, mainly from infectious disease. The National University of San Marcos was founded in Lima in 1551. Peru proclaimed independence in 1821 and completed it in 1824, with the battle of Ayacucho. Guano exploitation brought relative stability until the War of the Pacific, 1879–1884.

Peru is a unitary semi-presidential republic under its 1993 constitution, with a president elected for five years without immediate re-election. The population was 33,396,698 in estimates to 2022, about 80 percent of them urban, and the Lima metropolitan area has over 9.8 million people. Spanish is the main language, but many Peruvians speak Quechuan languages, Aymara or other Indigenous languages.
peter-tordenskjold: Peter Jansen Wessel was the tenth child of the Trondheim alderman Jan Wessel. An unruly boy, he stowed away on a ship to Copenhagen in 1704 and tried without success to become a naval cadet. The king's chaplain, Peder Jespersen, sent him on a voyage to the West Indies and at last found him a cadetship. After voyages to the East Indies he was made second lieutenant on 7 July 1711. The Norwegian admiral Waldemar Løvendal gave him the four-gun sloop Ormen and in June 1712 the 18-gun Løvendals Galej, against the advice of the Danish admiralty, which thought him unreliable.

He took part in the destruction of Swedish transports at Rügen on 29 September 1712. On 26 and 27 July 1714, off Lindesnes, he fought the 28-gun Swedish privateer Olbing Galley until both ships were badly damaged, then sent to thank her crew and to ask for more ammunition so as to go on. King Frederick IV had him court-martialled for disclosing his lack of ammunition and for risking his ship against a stronger one; he was acquitted on 15 December and made captain on 28 December.

At Kolberg on 24 April 1715 he captured the Swedish Rear-Admiral Hans Wachtmeister and the frigate Hvita Örn, which became his flagship. At Dynekilen on 8 July 1716, with two frigates and five smaller ships, he took or destroyed around 30 Swedish vessels. A failure against the Gothenburg squadron in 1717 brought a second court-martial in 1718, which was quashed after Ulrik Christian Gyldenløve intervened. He became rear-admiral in December 1718 and vice-admiral after partly destroying and partly capturing the Gothenburg squadron on 26 September 1719.

On 12 November 1720, aged 30, he was killed by the sword of the Livonian colonel Jakob Axel Staël von Holstein in a duel at Gleidingen near Hildesheim. The quarrel arose at a dinner where Tordenskiold spoke of a friend cheated at gambling. As duelling was against Danish law, his body was brought to Holmen Church without much ceremony. He is named in the Danish anthem Kong Christian stod ved højen mast of 1778 and the Norwegian anthem Ja, vi elsker dette landet of 1864. A story that at Marstrand his men moved from post to post to seem more numerous gave Danish and Norwegian the phrase Tordenskjold's soldiers.
philippines: The Philippines consists of about 7,641 islands with a total area of about 300,000 km2, stretching 1,850 kilometres from north to south. They fall into three divisions, Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao, and the 11 largest islands make up about 95 percent of the land. The highest mountain is Mount Apo on Mindanao, at 2,954 metres.

The islands lie on the western fringes of the Pacific Ring of Fire, with 23 active volcanoes and about five recorded earthquakes a day, most too weak to be felt. In 1542 Ruy López de Villalobos named Leyte and Samar Felipinas after the Prince of Asturias, later Philip II of Castile, and the name Las Islas Filipinas was later used for the Spanish possessions. The title Republic of the Philippines appeared in the 1935 constitution.

Evidence of early hominins dates to as early as 709,000 years ago, and bones from Callao Cave may represent an unknown species, Homo luzonensis, who lived 50,000 to 67,000 years ago. The first Austronesians reached the islands from Taiwan around 2200 BCE and settled the Batanes Islands and northern Luzon. The earliest known surviving written record is the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 CE, in Old Malay. By the 14th century large coastal settlements had become trading centres, trade with China had begun under the late Tang dynasty and widened under the Song, and Islam was established in the Sulu Archipelago by the 15th century.

Ferdinand Magellan's arrival marked the beginning of Spanish colonization. Catholicism became the dominant religion, and Manila became the western hub of trans-Pacific trade. The Philippine Revolution began in 1896 and became entwined with the Spanish–American War of 1898, after which Spain ceded the territory to the United States and revolutionaries declared the First Philippine Republic. The ensuing Philippine–American War left the United States in control until the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.

Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law from 1972 to 1981, and the People Power Revolution overthrew him in 1986. The Philippines is a constitutional republic with a presidential system, in which the president serves a six-year term, and its population was 112,729,484 in July 2024. The largest ethnic group in the 2020 census was the Tagalog, at 26.0 percent, and indigenous peoples comprise 110 ethnolinguistic groups. Spanish and American rule left lasting marks, among them the dominance of Catholicism, the use of English and Spanish surnames resulting from an 1849 edict.
plato: Plato was born between 428 and 423 BCE into an aristocratic and influential Athenian family. Through his mother, Perictione, he was a descendant of Solon, the statesman credited with laying the foundations of Athenian democracy. Diogenes Laertius asserted that Plato was a nickname alluding to his robust figure and that his birth name was Aristocles, but modern scholarship widely regards this as false. His brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus appear in the Republic. During his childhood Athens was at war with Sparta in the Peloponnesian War, and both brothers distinguished themselves at the battle of Megara in 409 BCE.

Like all male citizens of Athens, Plato received a traditional education in gymnastics and music. Ancient writers report a tradition that in his youth he wrote poems and tragedies, but burnt them when he met Socrates and turned to philosophy. He soon became a member of Socrates' inner circle. Socrates examined the ideas of his interlocutors by a series of questions, the Socratic method, and turned philosophy from natural philosophy to questions of ethics and politics.

Plato wrote dialogues in which Socrates is usually the primary speaker. Plato never presents himself as a participant. The dialogues discuss religion, human nature, love, perception and reality, and body and soul. His best known contribution is the theory of Forms, first introduced in the Phaedo. It holds that there is an apparent world of material objects grasped by the senses, which constantly changes, and an unchanging and unseen world of Forms, grasped by reason. He also argued for the immortality of the soul, and in the Republic the soul has three parts.

Thirty-five dialogues and thirteen letters have traditionally been ascribed to Plato, though modern scholarship doubts the authenticity of at least some of them. No one knows the exact order in which the dialogues were written. During the Islamic Golden Age, Neoplatonism was revived, and Al-Farabi, inspired by the Republic, proposed an ideal city governed by philosopher-kings. Byzantine scholars reintroduced Plato's texts to Western Europe in the early Renaissance, and about 250 Byzantine manuscripts survive. The edition published by Henricus Stephanus in Geneva in 1578 established the standard Stephanus pagination still in use.
poland: Poland covers an administrative area of 312,722 square kilometres, the ninth-largest country in Europe. The central and northern parts bordering the Baltic Sea lie within the flat Central European Plain, while the south is hilly and mountainous. The Sudetes lie in the west and the Carpathians in the east, and the Tatra Mountains hold the highest point, the northwestern summit of Rysy at 2,500 metres. The coastline spans 770 kilometres. The longest rivers are the Vistula, the Oder, the Warta and the Bug, and the country has around ten thousand lakes, mostly in the north-eastern region of Masuria.

The first Stone Age archaic humans settled the area approximately 500,000 years ago. The earliest evidence of European cheesemaking, from 5500 BCE, was discovered in Kuyavia, and a fortified settlement at Biskupin is attributed to the Lusatian culture of the Late Bronze Age. In antiquity many peoples lived in the territory, among them Celtic, Scythian, Germanic, Sarmatian, Baltic and Slavic tribes. Poland began to form into a unitary and territorial entity around the middle of the 10th century under the Piast dynasty, and in 966 the ruler of the Polans, Mieszko I, accepted Western Christianity under the Roman Catholic Church. The Kingdom of Poland emerged in 1025.

In 1569 Poland cemented its long-standing association with Lithuania, forming the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had an elective monarchy and adopted Europe's first modern constitution in 1791. The country was partitioned by neighbouring states at the end of the 18th century and regained independence in 1918 as the Second Polish Republic.

The invasion of Poland by Germany and by the Soviet Union in September 1939 marked the beginning of World War II, which resulted in the Holocaust and millions of Polish casualties. Forced into the Eastern Bloc, the Polish People's Republic was a signatory of the Warsaw Pact. The Solidarity movement emerged in 1980, and in 1989 Poland re-established itself as a liberal democracy and held free elections.

Poland has over 37 million people and is composed of sixteen voivodeships, with Warsaw as its capital and largest city. It is a unitary parliamentary republic with a bicameral legislature of the Sejm, with 460 members, and the Senate, with 100. The 2021 census found that ethnic Poles comprise 98.84% of the population. It keeps its own currency, the złoty. Poland has 18 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
portuguese-language: Portuguese belongs to the Ibero-Romance group, which evolved from several dialects of Vulgar Latin in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia and the County of Portugal. Before the Roman conquest the territory of modern Portugal was inhabited by the Gallaeci, Lusitanians, Celts, Iberians, Phoenicians, Greeks and Ligurians, whose languages were gradually replaced but left words behind, many of them about nature, agriculture and material culture. The Roman presence began in 218 BCE and full consolidation came in 19 BCE under Augustus. Latin spread outward from the cities and was tied to Roman citizenship. In the 5th century the Suebi and Visigoths conquered the peninsula and contributed about 500 Germanic words, many to do with warfare.

Portuguese has a rich system of nasal vowels, and its spelling is largely phonemic but shaped by etymology and tradition. Its verbs have kept more inflections from classical Latin than any other major Romance language, and it has features that other Romance languages, except Galician and Fala, lack, among them the future subjunctive and the personal infinitive. Its lexicon of around 228,500 entries comes largely from Latin, with more than 3,000 words traced to pre-Roman Celtic sources and loanwords from Germanic, Arabic, African, Amerindian and Asian languages. It is fully mutually intelligible with Galician, with which it shares its origin in the medieval language Galician-Portuguese. Two standard varieties are used for learning, European and Brazilian Portuguese.

Colonial expansion carried Portuguese across the world. It is the official language of eight countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe and Timor-Leste, and shares official status in Macau and Equatorial Guinea. There are about 267 million speakers in all, some 200 million of them in South America and 30 million in Africa. In Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau a Portuguese-based creole is also widely spoken. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries unites all the officially Lusophone nations, and recent spelling agreements have tried to give the language one spelling everywhere.
prague: Prague is situated on the Vltava River, into which the Berounka flows in the suburb of Lahovice. Most of the city lies on the Prague Plateau. Its highest point is the hill Teleček on the western border, at 399 metres, and its lowest is the Vltava at Suchdol, at 172 metres. The city grew from a settlement stretching from Prague Castle in the north to the fort of Vyšehrad in the south. Its archaeological deposits are over 10 metres deep. The name Praha has been explained in several ways, among them as meaning a threshold, a ford or rapid, or a burned forest cleared for settlement.

The region was settled as early as the Paleolithic. Around the fifth and fourth centuries BCE a Celtic tribe, the Boii, appeared there and gave Bohemia its name, meaning home of the Boii. They built the largest Celtic oppidum in Bohemia, at Závist, and in the last century BCE Germanic tribes slowly drove them out. The 2nd-century map of Ptolemaios mentions a Germanic city called Casurgis near the site of present-day Prague.

Prague became the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia and the residence of several Holy Roman Emperors, most notably Charles IV, who reigned from 1346 to 1378, and Rudolf II, who reigned from 1575 to 1611. Charles University, founded in 1348, is the oldest university in Central Europe. The city played major roles in the Bohemian and Protestant Reformations and in the Thirty Years' War. It was an important city to the Habsburg monarchy and to Austria-Hungary, and the capital of Czechoslovakia in the interwar period and in the Communist era after World War II.

Prague suffered considerably less damage in World War II than some other major cities in the region, which allowed most of its historic architecture to stay true to form. The city contains buildings in many styles, from Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque to Art Nouveau and Cubist. The Estates Theatre was the venue of the premieres of Mozart's Don Giovanni and La clemenza di Tito.

Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic and the historical capital of Bohemia, with a population of about 1.4 million. It has had the status of a statutory city again since 24 November 1990. The historic centre has been on the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites since 1992. Among its landmarks are Prague Castle, Charles Bridge, the Old Town Square with the astronomical clock, the Jewish Quarter and Vyšehrad. It has been nicknamed the City of a Hundred Spires.
prince-vijaya: The Mahavamsa gives Vijaya a marvellous ancestry. His grandmother Suppadevi, daughter of the king of Vanga and a princess of Kalinga, was carried off by Sinha, the lion, whom some modern interpreters take to have been an outlaw living in the forest. Their son Sinhabahu escaped with his mother and sister, killed his father, founded the city of Sinhapura in the Lala country and married his sister Sinhasivali. Vijaya was the eldest of their thirty-two sons. Where Sinhapura lay is uncertain: it has been placed in Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, among other places.

Made prince regent by his father, Vijaya became notorious with his followers for violent deeds, and prominent citizens demanded his death. Sinhabahu instead expelled them: their heads were half shaved and they were put on a ship, their wives and children being sent off on separate ships.

In the Mahavamsa's telling the kingdom was named Tambapanni, copper-red hands, because the red soil coloured the hands of Vijaya's men, and his people were called Sinhala after Sinhabahu. His ministers founded villages, among them Upatissagama. To be crowned he needed a queen of noble house, and the Pandya king of Madhura, identified with Madurai, sent his daughter with a hundred noble maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of eighteen guilds, who landed at the port of Mahatittha.

Vijaya then sent Kuveni away, since his people feared supernatural beings. She went with their two children, Jivahatta and Disala, to the Yakkha city of Lankapura, where she was killed as a traitor. The children fled to Sumanakuta, and from them the chronicle derives the Pulinda, identified with the Vedda people. Vijaya, crowned, is said to have given up his evil ways and ruled in peace and justice.

Having no heir, Vijaya in old age sent for his twin brother Sumitta, but died before a reply came. His ministers governed for a year until Panduvasudeva, Sumitta's youngest son, arrived from Sinhapura to rule. The older Dipavamsa tells a similar story without Kuveni or the South Indian princess, and two other versions of the legend, one recorded by Xuanzang and one a Jataka painted at Ajanta, give the founding prince other names.

There is no archaeological evidence for the story. In Sri Lanka it is often treated as history and used in political argument: Sinhalese scholars such as K. M. de Silva have cited it for the Indo-Aryan origins of the Sinhalese, while Tamil authors such as Satchi Ponnambalam have dismissed it as fiction serving Sinhalese territorial claims.
punctation-of-olmutz: The German Confederation, dominated by Austria, had been dissolved in the Revolutions of 1848 and partially succeeded by the Frankfurt Assembly. After the assembly failed, Prussia took the initiative in early 1850 with the Erfurt Union, a federation of most of the German states under its own lead. The two powers were thus in conflict over the leadership of Germany.

A dispute between the Elector of Hesse and his subjects gave the Austrian chancellor Felix zu Schwarzenberg the occasion to isolate Prussia further. Austrian and allied armies advanced into the Electorate of Hesse, and on 8 November 1850 the Prussian army came close to war with Bavaria, an ally of Austria, near Fulda-Bronnzell. In the Warsaw negotiations of October 1850 Tsar Nicholas I of Russia had already taken Austria's side, which was part of the reason why Prussia decided to give in.

The agreement, also called the Agreement of Olmütz, came out of a conference held in the town, now Olomouc in the Czech Republic, and closed the Autumn Crisis of 1850. Prussia gave up its claim to lead the German states and submitted to Austrian leadership of the restored confederation. It agreed to demobilise, to take part in the intervention of the German Diet in Hesse and in Holstein, and renounced any resumption of the Erfurt Union. Austria for its part agreed to call a conference of ministers to discuss a reform of the confederation.

The ministerial conference that Austria had promised met in Dresden the following year and ended without result, so that the confederation continued unreformed under Austrian leadership. The name of humiliation was given to the treaty because many saw in it a capitulation of the Prussians to the Austrians.
purandar-singha: Purandar Singha was born in 1807 at Silmari in British-ruled Bengal, a great-great-grandson of the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha. His grandfather and his father Brajanath Gohain had conspired against reigning kings and lived there as exiled princes in poverty. In 1818 Ruchinath Burhagohain, who held King Chandrakanta Singha responsible for bringing in the Burmese, invited Brajanath to claim the throne, and their force entered the capital Jorhat on 17 February 1818. Brajanath had coins struck in his own name, but the mutilation of one of his ears barred him from kingship, since an Ahom king had to be without blemish. His son, then ten years old, was acclaimed instead.

Real authority lay with Brajanath and Ruchinath, who removed the officers suspected of loyalty to Chandrakanta. A Burmese army of 30,000 sent by King Bodawpaya defeated the Assamese on 17 February 1819; Purandar, his father and Ruchinath fled to Guwahati with the valuables of the royal treasury, worth 3.5 million rupees. After a second defeat on 11 June 1819 they escaped to Bengal. The Governor-General Lord Hastings refused to help. They recruited soldiers in Goalpara, Bengal and Bhutan, armed with the aid of a British trader, Robert Bruce, and fought both Chandrakanta and the Burmese before withdrawing in 1822.

After the Treaty of Yandabo of 24 February 1826 the British held the Brahmaputra valley. Sensing discontent, they considered in 1832 restoring Upper Assam as a tributary princedom and chose Purandar over Chandrakanta; some historians think they expected a long-exiled prince to be the more grateful and submissive. From April 1833 he ruled from Jorhat, without Sadiya and Matak, for a tribute of 50,000 rupees. Within three years he fell behind in his payments and asked for a reduction. An enquiry by Captain Francis Jenkins found corruption and oppression, and the king himself amassing a personal fortune.

The kingdom was placed under direct British control in September 1838. Purandar stayed in Jorhat and refused the pension of 1,000 rupees a month granted in October 1838, hoping that a petition to the Governor-General would restore his state; it was turned down. When officials and adventurers dug into the royal tombs, the maidams, at Charaideo in search of treasure, he first protested and then opened many tombs himself. He died on 1 October 1846 and was entombed at Jorhat, at the place now called Raja Maidam.
